name: ntfs-file-recovery
description: >-
  Recover files deleted from a Windows NTFS drive when no backup, Shadow Copy, or
  Recycle Bin entry survives, and diagnose what deleted them. Use when files
  vanish from a drive after a mass deletion, an agent or script ran a recursive
  delete, a suspected junction/loop caused a tree to be wiped, or the user asks
  "how do I get my files back" / "what deleted my files". Covers NTFS $MFT
  parsing with no third-party tools, USN Journal forensics, PowerShell event-log
  root-causing, and junction/symlink footguns in `rd /s /q` and `Remove-Item -Recurse`.
---

# NTFS File Recovery

Two jobs that belong together: **prove what happened**, then **get the files back**.
Do them in that order — knowing the deletion mechanism tells you which data is
still intact and whether the source volume is safe to write to.

## Golden rules

0. **Run elevated.** Raw disk access (`\\.\PhysicalDriveN`) needs an
   Administrator shell; a medium-integrity shell fails with
   `ERROR_ACCESS_DENIED` (5). In PowerShell:
   `Start-Process powershell -Verb RunAs -ArgumentList "-NoProfile","-Command","python scripts\ntfs_recover.py ..."`.
   Read-only inspection of the volume (PowerShell, `fsutil`, event logs) does
   not require elevation.
1. **Never write to the source volume.** Every byte you write can overwrite the
   clusters holding files you have not recovered yet. Recover to a *different*
   volume. If only one volume exists, recover to a network share or an external
   disk, and stop writing to the source entirely until you are done.
2. **Diagnose before recovering.** The deletion mechanism determines whether the
   MFT records still point at live data or have already been recycled.
3. **Read the MFT before you trust a tool.** `$MFT` holds the filename, the
   parent reference, the size and the data-run list for every file, deleted or
   not, until those records get reused. That is often weeks of data with no
   third-party tool and no backup.

## Phase 1 — Triage (read-only)

Run `scripts/triage.ps1 -Drive E`. It reports, without modifying anything:

- USN Journal window and the deleted-file timeline (alphabetical walk order
  across top-level folders is the signature of a recursive delete)
- PowerShell `Windows PowerShell` log entries whose `HostApplication` contains a
  destructive command, plus `Microsoft-Windows-PowerShell/Operational` 4104
  script-block bodies if script-block logging is on
- Shadow Copies / File History / Windows Backup availability
- Recycle Bin integrity (`$I`/`$R` pair validity) and orphaned `$I`/`$R` files
- Directory junctions and reparse points on the volume — see the footgun below

Read the timeline top-to-bottom before touching anything. The gap between the
last clean command and the first delete usually names the culprit exactly.

## Phase 2 — Recover from the MFT

Run `scripts/ntfs_recover.py`:

```
python ntfs_recover.py --drive E --list                 # inventory of deleted files
python ntfs_recover.py --drive E --out F:\recovered --by-size-desc
python ntfs_recover.py --drive E --out F:\recovered --match "\.pdf$" --match "DOKUMENTASI"
```

It parses the boot sector, locates `$MFT` (including multi-run `$MFT`),
reconstructs each deleted file's path from parent file references, and copies the
data out of the recorded clusters. Output keeps the original directory tree.

Critical details it already handles (do not re-derive these):

- **FRN masking.** A file reference is 48 bits of record number plus 16 bits of
  sequence number. Compare `frn & 0xFFFFFFFFFFFF` against the record index, or
  every parent lookup silently fails and all paths collapse to one bucket.
- **Long vs 8.3 names.** A directory can carry both a short name and a long
  name in separate `$FILE_NAME` attributes. Prefer the long name (namespace 1 or
  3) when rebuilding paths, or you get `PROGRA~2` instead of `Program Files (x86)`.
- **Size is not the truth.** Trust the run list for byte count. `$FILE_NAME`
  sizes can be stale or zero for deleted records; a run list claiming 2^60
  clusters means the record was recycled and the file is unrecoverable.
- **Validate every run list** (run length within sane bounds, LCN inside the
  volume, total bytes consistent with the recorded size). A corrupt run list
  produces a gigantic file that fills the destination and hides real data.

Order extraction by **starting LCN, not by name**. On spinning or SMR drives
that turns thousands of random seeks into a near-sequential pass; the difference
measured here was 3 MB/s versus 140 MB/s on the same data.

### Verify what came out

Check magic bytes before trusting a recovered file: `%PDF` for PDF, `\xFF\xD8\xFF`
for JPEG, `\x89PNG` for PNG, `SFPK`/`SBPK` for sPackage, `ftyp` for MP4/MOV,
`PE\0\0` for DLL/EXE. Sample a few hundred files and report the hit rate. Flag
the rest rather than claiming success.

## The junction footgun (this causes whole-drive wipes)

`cmd.exe`'s `rd /s /q` and PowerShell's `Remove-Item -Recurse` behave
differently on **directory junctions and symlinks**:

- `rd /s /q <junction>` walks **through** the junction and deletes the
  *target's* contents. Point it at a junction to a drive root and it wipes the
  root.
- `Remove-Item -Recurse` on a junction removes the link, not the target.

Evidence that a junction caused a wipe: deleted paths are reported under the
junction path in the USN Journal, while the `$MFT` parent references point at
the real location. Both views are correct — the junction is a reparse point and
NTFS records the traversal through it.

**Always enumerate reparse points before running any recursive delete**, and
resolve them to their real targets before quoting a path in a command. If a
target path looks like a drive root, stop.

## Restore-in-place ordering

If the recovered files must go back to the volume they came from, extract
everything to another volume first, then copy back. Writing to the source while
still reading clusters from it lets the allocator hand you back clusters that
hold not-yet-recovered files.

## Reference

`reference/ntfs-layout.md` — boot sector fields, MFT record layout, attribute
headers, run-list encoding, and the FRN/sequence-number rule.

## Real-world impact

A 742 GB restore on a drive whose entire contents had been wiped was recovered
at 99.1% file success from `$MFT` alone — no backup, no Shadow Copy, no
commercial tool — because the MFT records had not yet been recycled. The
remaining 0.9% was game-engine binaries and archive files that had been
re-downloaded since the deletion and were therefore genuinely overwritten.

# 🛟 ntfs-file-recovery

Pulihkan file yang terhapus dari drive Windows **NTFS** — tanpa tool komersial,
tanpa backup, tanpa Shadow Copy. Plus forensik: **siapa** yang menghapusnya.

Berbasis teknik yang dipakai untuk memulihkan **742 GB / 189.949 file** dari
drive E: yang isinya wiped total oleh `rd /s /q` yang mengikuti junction.

| | |
| --- | --- |
| Bahasa | Python 3 (stdlib saja) + PowerShell |
| Dependensi | Tidak ada (`ctypes` saja untuk raw disk read) |
| Root | Admin / elevated shell wajib untuk akses `\\.\PhysicalDriveN` |
| Lisensi | MIT — lihat [`LICENSE`](LICENSE) |

## Kenapa skill ini ada

Pada 21 Oktober 2026 sebuah `cmd /c "rmdir /s /q ..."` dengan escaping rusak
menyapu **591 GB** dari drive E:. Tidak ada backup, tidak ada Shadow Copy, tidak
ada recycle bin. Satu-satunya sumber data yang masih utuh adalah **MFT** NTFS
itu sendiri.

Hasilnya: **99,1% file berhasil dipulihkan** (nama, path, dan isi utuh),
karena record MFT-nya belum sempat didaur ulang.

## Yang dicakup

1. **Forensik dulu** — USN Journal, log PowerShell, cek Shadow Copy, cek
   recycle bin, deteksi junction.
2. **Pemulihan dari `$MFT`** — parser NTFS dari nol: boot sector → `$MFT` →
   rekonstruksi path via parent reference → ekstrak isi dari run list.
3. **Validasi** — magic byte per ekstensi, Sampling hundreds of files and
   reporting the hit rate instead of claiming success.
4. **Footgun junction** — kenapa `rd /s /q` bisa menghapus SELURUH isi drive.

## Pemakaian

### 1. Forensik (read-only, tidak perlu admin)

```powershell
.\scripts\triage.ps1 -Drive E
```

Menghasilkan: timeline USN Journal, perintah destruktif di log PowerShell,
status Shadow Copy/Windows Backup, integritas recycle bin, dan daftar
junction/reparse point.

### 2. Inventaris file yang terhapus

```powershell
python scripts\ntfs_recover.py --drive E --list
python scripts\ntfs_recover.py --drive E --list --match "\.pdf$" --match "DOKUMENTASI"
python scripts\ntfs_recover.py --drive E --list --index-out inventory.json
```

### 3. Ekstraksi

```powershell
# WAJIB elevated
python scripts\ntfs_recover.py --drive E --out F:\recovered
python scripts\ntfs_recover.py --drive E --out F:\recovered --by-size-desc --verify
```

> **Jangan pernah menulis ke drive sumber.** Tiap byte yang ditulis bisa
> menimpa cluster file yang belum sempat dipulihkan. Script menolak menulis ke
> drive yang sama.

## Cara kerjanya

| Tahap | Isi |
| --- | --- |
| Boot sector | bytes/sector, sectors/cluster, LCN `$MFT`, ukuran record |
| `$MFT` | run list sendiri (bisa multi-run) → peta offset |
| Record | header flag (in-use / directory), `$FILE_NAME`, `$DATA` |
| Path | naik lewat parent FRN;FRN = 48 bit index + 16 bit sequence → **mask `& 0xFFFFFFFFFFFF`** |
| Nama | pilih namespace 1/3 (panjang) sebelum namespace 2 (8.3) |
| Ukuran | dari run list, bukan `$FILE_NAME` (bisa basi / nol) |
| Validasi | panjang run ≤ 2^26 cluster, LCN dalam volume, total cocok dengan size |
| Extract | urut **LCN menaik** → baca disk nyaris sekuensial |

Detail teknis ada di [`reference/ntfs-layout.md`](reference/ntfs-layout.md).

## Jebakan yang harus diketahui

- **Junction + `rd /s /q` = hapus isi drive.**
  `cmd.exe` menelusuri *melewati* junction dan menghapus isi targetnya.
  `Remove-Item -Recurse` (PowerShell) menghapus link-nya saja.
  Kalau path targetnya terlihat seperti root drive — berhenti.
- **Powershell tidak meng-escape `\"` di dalam string berkoma dua.**
  `cmd /c "rmdir /s /q \"C:\path\""` terpotong jadi beberapa argumen.
  Pakai backtick (`` `" ``) atau `--%`.
- **Record MFT bisa didaur ulang** begitu slot-nya dipakai file baru.
  Quanto cepat recovery dimulai, semakin besar peluang datanya masih ada.
- **Checksum / magic byte harus dicek.** File dengan CRC/size cocok tapi isi
  sudah tertimpa akan lolos validasi nama.

# NTFS structures used by the recovery tool

Everything here is what `scripts/ntfs_recover.py` reads. Values are little-endian.

## Boot sector (offset 0 of the partition)

| Offset | Size | Field |
|---|---|---|
| 0x03 | 8 | OEM ID (`NTFS    `) |
| 0x0B | 2 | bytes per sector |
| 0x0D | 1 | sectors per cluster |
| 0x28 | 8 | total sectors |
| 0x30 | 8 | `$MFT` starting cluster (LCN) |
| 0x38 | 8 | `$MFTMirr` starting LCN |
| 0x40 | 1 | clusters per MFT record (signed): positive = count, negative = 2^-n bytes |

## MFT record (1024 bytes typical)

| Offset | Size | Field |
|---|---|---|
| 0x00 | 4 | magic `FILE` |
| 0x04 | 2 | update sequence array offset |
| 0x06 | 2 | update sequence array count |
| 0x10 | 2 | sequence number |
| 0x12 | 2 | hard link count |
| 0x14 | 2 | offset to first attribute |
| 0x16 | 2 | flags: bit0 = in use, bit1 = directory |
| 0x20 | 8 | base record reference (non-zero = this record extends another) |
| 0x2C | 4 | MFT record number |

Attribute headers follow the first-attribute offset.

| Resident | Non-resident |
|---|---|
| 0x00 type (4) | 0x00 type (4) |
| 0x04 length (4) | 0x04 length (4) |
| 0x08 non-resident flag (0) | 0x08 non-resident flag (1) |
| 0x09 name length | 0x09 name length |
| 0x0A name offset | 0x0A name offset |
| 0x0C flags | 0x0C flags (bit0 = compressed) |
| 0x0E attribute id | 0x0E attribute id |
| 0x10 value length (4) | 0x10 lowest VCN (8) |
| 0x14 value offset (2) | 0x18 highest VCN (8) |
| 0x16 value flags (1) | 0x20 run list offset (2) |
| | 0x28 allocated size (8) |
| | 0x30 real size (8) |
| | 0x38 initialized size (8) |

Attribute types: `0x10` `$STANDARD_INFORMATION`, `0x20` `$ATTRIBUTE_LIST`,
`0x30` `$FILE_NAME`, `0x80` `$DATA`.

## `$FILE_NAME` value

| Offset | Size | Field |
|---|---|---|
| 0x00 | 8 | parent file reference (FRN) |
| 0x08 | 8 | creation time (FILETIME) |
| 0x10 | 8 | modification time |
| 0x18 | 8 | MFT change time |
| 0x20 | 8 | access time |
| 0x28 | 8 | allocated size |
| 0x30 | 8 | real data size |
| 0x38 | 4 | flags |
| 0x3C | 4 | reparse tag |
| 0x40 | 1 | file name length (chars) |
| 0x41 | 1 | namespace: 0 = POSIX, 1 = Win32, 2 = DOS 8.3, 3 = Win32 + POSIX |
| 0x42 | var | name, UTF-16LE |

**Namespace 2 is the 8.3 short name.** A long file usually has two
`$FILE_NAME` attributes: one namespace 3 (long) and one namespace 2 (short).
Pick namespace 3/1 first when rebuilding paths, or every path comes out as
`PROGRA~2` and `DOKUME~1`.

## File reference numbers (FRN)

A reference is **48 bits of MFT record number + 16 bits of sequence number**:

```
record_index = frn & 0xFFFFFFFFFFFF
sequence     = frn >> 48
```

Comparing an unmasked FRN against a record index silently fails, and every
parent lookup then resolves to nothing — all files collapse into one bucket
named after the volume root. This is the single most common bug in hand-rolled
MFT readers.

## Run list encoding

A run list is a sequence of header bytes, each followed by a length field and
optionally a signed LCN delta:

```
header byte:  bits 0-3 = length field size
              bits 4-7 = offset field size
length:       little-endian unsigned, in clusters
offset:       little-endian SIGNED, delta from the previous LCN
```

An offset field size of 0 means the run is a **sparse hole** (read as zeros).
A terminating `0x00` header ends the list.

Total bytes = sum(run_length) x cluster_size.

**Recycled records** keep a stale run list with absurd lengths. Validate before
copying: run length <= 2^26 clusters, LCN inside the volume, and total bytes
consistent with the recorded real size. An unvalidated run list produces a
multi-terabyte file that fills the destination and buries the real data.

## Deleted-record semantics

- The record header's in-use bit is cleared, but the attributes remain.
- The record is only overwritten when the MFT slot is **reused**. A record
  whose base record reference is non-zero is an extension of another record,
  not an independent file.
- Once reused, the original name and run list are gone. That is the boundary
  between recoverable and not, and it is why recovery should start before the
  volume fills up with new data.

## Reconstructing a path

Follow parent FRNs from the file's `$FILE_NAME` attribute up to the volume
root, collecting names. A parent record that was deleted and its slot reused
breaks the chain: the file still exists but its path can no longer be derived.
Both the USN Journal and the MFT can supply the chain; the USN Journal records
the traversal **through reparse points**, so a junction shows up as an extra
path segment that the MFT parent references do not contain. Both views are
correct and they are how you detect that a junction was involved.

## Volume layout

| Offset | Size | Field |
|---|---|---|
| 0x00 | 3 | jump instruction |
| 0x03 | 8 | OEM ID |
| 0x0B | 2 | bytes per sector |
| 0x0D | 1 | sectors per cluster |
| 0x28 | 8 | total sectors |
| 0x30 | 8 | `$MFT` LCN |
| 0x38 | 8 | `$MFTMirr` LCN |
| 0x40 | 1 | clusters per MFT record (signed) |
| 0x50 | 8 | volume serial number |
| 0x68 | 8 | MFT zone / reserved |

`$MFT` itself is usually a non-resident file with its own run list; read the
run list from MFT record 0 instead of assuming a contiguous layout.

## Reading raw

Open `\\.\PhysicalDriveN` with `GENERIC_READ` and `FILE_SHARE_READ|FILE_SHARE_WRITE`.
Reads must be **sector aligned** — a misaligned `ReadFile` on a raw device fails
with `ERROR_INVALID_PARAMETER` (87). Set the file pointer with `SetFilePointerEx`
and read with `ReadFile`; `os.pread` does not exist on Windows.
